sine-generator.title: Sine Generator
sine-generator.purpose: Generates a continuous sinusoidal signal of the form s(t) = A · sin(2π·f·t + φ). This is the most basic block in digital signal processing, used as a test signal, carrier frequency, reference tone, and building block for complex signals.
sine-generator.algorithm: Uses a phase accumulator — at each sample the phase is incremented by Δφ = 2π·f / sampleRate. The sine value is computed as Math.sin(currentPhase + phaseOffset). The phase is normalized to the range [0, 2π) to prevent precision loss during prolonged operation. The accumulator preserves state between chunks, ensuring signal continuity without clicks or discontinuities.

frequency.description: sine wave frequency in Hz. Valid range: 0 to sampleRate/2 (Nyquist limit, typically up to 24000 Hz). Typical values: 440 (note A), 1000 (test tone), 10000 (carrier).

amplitude.description: signal amplitude. Range: 0.0–1.0. Values > 1.0 are allowed but may cause clipping when played through Speaker. A value of 0 produces silence.

phase.description: initial phase offset in degrees. Range: 0–360°. Converted to radians: phaseOffset = phase · π/180. Used to set the initial phase, e.g., 90° turns a sine into a cosine.

examples.title: Spectral analysis of a sum of tones
examples.description: Sine(1000 Hz) + Sine(3000 Hz) → Summer → SpectrumAnalyzer Two peaks are visible on the spectrum: at 1 kHz and 3 kHz.

examples.title: Carrier modulation
examples.description: Sine(100 Hz, amplitude 0.5) → AMFMPMModulator(FM, carrier 10000 Hz) The 100 Hz sine wave is used as a modulating signal for FM modulation.

examples.title: Filter testing
examples.description: Sine(5000 Hz) → LowpassFIR(cutoff 3000 Hz) → Oscilloscope The 5 kHz signal is suppressed by the filter — the output is nearly silence.

cosine-generator.title: Cosine Generator
cosine-generator.purpose: Generates a continuous cosine signal of the form s(t) = A · cos(2π·f·t + φ). Cosine is the same as sine but shifted 90° (π/2 radians) ahead in phase. This signal is essential for forming quadrature pairs (I/Q), where sine represents the quadrature (Q) component and cosine represents the in-phase (I) component.
cosine-generator.algorithm: Identical to the sine generator, but uses Math.cos instead of Math.sin. The phase accumulator increments by Δφ = 2π·f / sampleRate each sample. The accumulator state is preserved between chunks for signal continuity. Phase is normalized to [0, 2π) to prevent float precision loss. Difference from the sine generator: cos(x) = sin(x + π/2). One could use the sine generator with phase=90°, but a separate cosine block is more convenient for diagram clarity and explicit quadrature signal generation.

frequency.description: cosine frequency in Hz. Valid range: 0 to sampleRate/2 (typically up to 24000 Hz).

amplitude.description: signal amplitude. Range: 0.0–1.0 (values > 1.0 are allowed but may cause clipping).

phase.description: initial phase offset in degrees. Range: 0–360°. Converted to radians: phaseOffset = phase · π/180.

examples.title: Orthogonality verification
examples.description: Sine(1000 Hz) → Multiplier ← Cosine(1000 Hz) → Integrator The integral of the sin·cos product over a whole number of periods approaches zero, confirming orthogonality.

examples.title: Coherent AM demodulation
examples.description: AMFMPMModulator(AM, carrier 10000 Hz) → Multiplier ← Cosine(10000 Hz) → LowpassFIR → Oscilloscope A cosine at the same frequency as the carrier is used for synchronous detection.

ref-sine-generator.title: Reference Sine Generator
ref-sine-generator.purpose: NCO (Numerically Controlled Oscillator) — a generator with external frequency and phase control. Unlike the regular sine generator, frequency and phase can be changed in real time via control inputs. This is a key block for building PLL (Phase-Locked Loop), coherent demodulators, adaptive filters, and frequency synthesis systems.
ref-sine-generator.algorithm: The phase accumulator is similar to the regular generator, but at each sample: 1. Instantaneous frequency is taken from the control input (or from the frequency parameter). 2. Phase offset is taken from the second input (or from the phase parameter). 3. Increment is computed: Δφ = 2π · freq / sampleRate. 4. Complex output is formed: I = sin(phase), Q = cos(phase). Phase is normalized to [0, 2π) to prevent precision loss during prolonged operation.
ref-sine-generator.inputDescription: - Input 0 'Frequency (Hz)' — instantaneous frequency, Hz. Each sample sets the frequency for the corresponding moment in time (enables frequency modulation). - Input 1 'Phase (rad)' — instantaneous phase offset, radians. Allows external phase correction (e.g., from a PLL loop filter).
ref-sine-generator.outputDescription: complex (interleaved Float32Array of length chunkSize × 2, I = sin, Q = cos)

frequency.description: base frequency in Hz. Used when the frequency input is not connected. Range: 0–sampleRate/2.

phase.description: base phase offset in degrees. Used when the phase input is not connected. Range: 0–360°.

examples.title: Controlled local oscillator (frequency shift)
examples.description: Constant(5000) → RefSine(frequency input) → ComplexMultiplier ← input signal NCO at a fixed frequency of 5 kHz is used for spectrum translation.

examples.title: Frequency modulation via NCO
examples.description: Sine(100 Hz) → Gain(1000) → RefSine(frequency input) → Oscilloscope The 100 Hz modulating signal controls the NCO frequency, creating an FM signal.

ref-cosine-generator.title: Reference Cosine Generator
ref-cosine-generator.purpose: NCO (Numerically Controlled Oscillator) with cosine quadrature. Similar to RefSine, but forms a complex output with different I/Q mapping: I = cos(φ), Q = −sin(φ). This corresponds to the complex exponential e^(−jφ), which is convenient for tasks requiring a conjugate reference signal (e.g., downconversion = multiplication by e^(−j·2π·f·t)).
ref-cosine-generator.algorithm: The phase accumulator is identical to RefSine. At each sample: 1. Instantaneous frequency is taken from the control input (or from the frequency parameter). 2. Phase offset is taken from the second input (or from the phase parameter). 3. Increment is computed: Δφ = 2π · freq / sampleRate. 4. Complex output is formed: I = cos(phase), Q = −sin(phase). Phase is normalized to [0, 2π). Difference from RefSine: RefSine: I = sin(φ), Q = cos(φ) → represents e^(jφ) (up to rotation) RefCosine: I = cos(φ), Q = −sin(φ) → represents e^(−jφ) When complex-multiplying the input signal by e^(−jφ), downconversion occurs (spectrum shifted down), which is necessary in receivers.
ref-cosine-generator.inputDescription: - Input 0 'Frequency (Hz)' — instantaneous frequency, Hz. - Input 1 'Phase (rad)' — instantaneous phase offset, radians.
ref-cosine-generator.outputDescription: complex (interleaved Float32Array of length chunkSize × 2, I = cos, Q = −sin)

frequency.description: base frequency in Hz. Used when the frequency input is not connected. Range: 0–sampleRate/2.

phase.description: base phase offset in degrees. Used when the phase input is not connected. Range: 0–360°.

examples.title: PLL with cosine NCO
examples.description: Signal → PhaseDetector → LoopFilter → → RefCosine(frequency input) → PhaseDetector (reference) Used when the phase detector expects a cosine reference signal.

examples.title: Comparing RefSine and RefCosine
examples.description: RefSine(1000 Hz) → Oscilloscope (channel 1) RefCosine(1000 Hz) → Oscilloscope (channel 2) The I-component of RefSine shows sin, the I-component of RefCosine shows cos.

audio-file.title: Audio File
audio-file.purpose: Allows loading a WAV file and using it as a real signal source in the processing graph. This is necessary for working with real recordings: speech analysis, music, radio signals, testing filters and detectors on real data instead of synthetic generators.
audio-file.algorithm: This plugin is a placeholder. The actual WAV file reading and feeding audio data into the graph is performed by DSPProcessor, which intercepts this block's processing and substitutes data from the loaded file. If for some reason process() is called directly (e.g., file not loaded), silence is returned (array of zeros). Supported format: WAV (PCM). Reading and decoding is performed by WavFileService. Stereo files are mixed down to mono. Sample rate is converted to the simulation's sampleRate.
audio-file.outputDescription: real (Float32Array of length chunkSize, data from WAV file or silence)

wavFile.description: File object selected by the user through the upload dialog. A null value means no file is loaded.

examples.title: Audio signal filtering
examples.description: AudioFile(music.wav) → BandpassFIR(200–3400 Hz) → Speaker Music is filtered by a bandpass filter (telephone band) and played back.

examples.title: Waterfall diagram
examples.description: AudioFile(radio.wav) → Waterfall Visualization of radio signal spectrum changes over time.

constant.title: Constant
constant.purpose: Generates a signal with a constant value at every sample. Used as: - DC offset (bias) — adding a DC component to a signal via Summer; - control signal — a fixed frequency value for NCO (RefSine/RefCosine); - scaling coefficient — multiplying a signal by a constant via Multiplier; - threshold level — setting a level for the Threshold block; - test signal — checking linearity and offset in a processing chain.
constant.algorithm: Trivial: the output Float32Array is filled with the same value using the fill() method. No state is stored between chunks (though a state Map is present for plugin interface compatibility).
constant.outputDescription: real (Float32Array of length chunkSize, filled with value)

value.description: constant value. Any float is allowed: positive, negative, zero values. Typical values: 0.0 (silence/zero), 1.0 (unity coefficient), 1000 (1 kHz frequency for NCO), −0.5 (negative offset).

examples.title: DC offset of a signal
examples.description: Sine(1000 Hz) + Constant(0.5) → Summer → Oscilloscope The sine wave is shifted up by 0.5, oscillating in the range [−0.5, 1.5].

examples.title: Scaling (manual Gain)
examples.description: Input signal → Multiplier ← Constant(0.1) The signal is attenuated by a factor of 10.

noise-generator.title: Noise Generator
noise-generator.purpose: Generates a pseudo-random noise signal of three types, each with its own spectral characteristics. Noise is used for testing filters (feeding a wideband signal and observing the frequency response at the output), modeling communication channels with additive noise, generating dithering signals, and as a source for studying statistical properties. Noise types and their spectral characteristics: - white (white noise) — flat spectrum, uniform power at all frequencies. Generated as Math.random() * 2 − 1 (uniform distribution [−1, 1]). Applications: filter frequency response testing, AWGN channel model, dithering. - pink (pink noise, 1/f) — power decreases inversely proportional to frequency. Each octave carries equal power (−3 dB/octave). Implementation: Paul Kellet filter — a cascade of 7 first-order IIR filters approximating the 1/f spectrum in the audio range. Output is normalized by a coefficient of 0.11 to bring amplitude to the ~±1 range. Applications: acoustic tests, flicker noise model, psychoacoustics. - brown (red/Brownian noise, 1/f²) — power decreases as 1/f² (−6 dB/octave). Similar to random walk (Brownian motion). Implementation: integration of white noise with limiting: brownLast += white · 0.02, with clipping to [−1, 1] to prevent drift. Applications: low-frequency fluctuation model, warm background generation.
noise-generator.algorithm: - white (white noise) — flat spectrum, uniform power at all frequencies. Generated as Math.random() * 2 − 1 (uniform distribution [−1, 1]). Applications: filter frequency response testing, AWGN channel model, dithering. - pink (pink noise, 1/f) — power decreases inversely proportional to frequency. Each octave carries equal power (−3 dB/octave). Implementation: Paul Kellet filter — a cascade of 7 first-order IIR filters approximating the 1/f spectrum in the audio range. Output is normalized by a coefficient of 0.11 to bring amplitude to the ~±1 range. Applications: acoustic tests, flicker noise model, psychoacoustics. - brown (red/Brownian noise, 1/f²) — power decreases as 1/f² (−6 dB/octave). Similar to random walk (Brownian motion). Implementation: integration of white noise with limiting: brownLast += white · 0.02, with clipping to [−1, 1] to prevent drift. Applications: low-frequency fluctuation model, warm background generation.

amplitude.description: amplitude (multiplier). Range: 0.0–1.0. Values > 1.0 are allowed but may cause clipping.

examples.title: Modeling a noisy channel
examples.description: Sine(1000 Hz) + NoiseGenerator(white, amplitude 0.1) → Summer → Oscilloscope A sine wave with added white noise — a model of a noisy signal.

examples.title: Comparing noise spectra
examples.description: NoiseGenerator(white) → SpectrumAnalyzer (flat spectrum) NoiseGenerator(pink) → SpectrumAnalyzer (3 dB/octave roll-off) NoiseGenerator(brown) → SpectrumAnalyzer (6 dB/octave roll-off)

examples.title: Testing correlation
examples.description: NoiseGenerator(white) → Correlator Autocorrelation of white noise produces a delta function (sharp peak at τ=0).

amfmpm-modulator.title: AM/FM/PM Modulator
amfmpm-modulator.purpose: Takes a modulating (information) signal and transfers it onto a high-frequency carrier using one of three methods: amplitude (AM), frequency (FM), or phase (PM) modulation. These are the basic types of analog modulation used in radio communications, broadcasting, and telemetry.
amfmpm-modulator.algorithm: Uses a phase accumulator with base increment Δφ = 2π · fc / sampleRate. - AM (amplitude modulation): s(t) = (1 + m · x(t)) · cos(φ) The carrier amplitude changes proportionally to the modulating signal x(t). At m=1 and x(t)=±1, modulation depth is 100%. At m > 1, overmodulation occurs (envelope distortion). Spectrum: carrier + two sidebands (fc ± fm). - FM (frequency modulation): s(t) = cos(φ), where φ += Δφ + 2π · m · x(t) / sampleRate The instantaneous frequency deviates from the carrier proportionally to x(t). Parameter m here is the frequency deviation (Hz): maximum frequency offset from the carrier when x(t)=1. Spectrum is wider than AM, bandwidth ≈ 2·(Δf + fm) (Carson's rule). - PM (phase modulation): s(t) = cos(φ + m · x(t)) The carrier phase shifts proportionally to x(t). Parameter m is the phase modulation index (radians): maximum phase shift when x(t)=1. PM is closely related to FM: FM = PM with an integrated modulating signal.
amfmpm-modulator.inputDescription: real (modulating signal, Float32Array). If input is not connected, x(t)=0 (unmodulated carrier).
amfmpm-modulator.outputDescription: real (modulated signal, Float32Array of length chunkSize)

carrierFrequency.description: carrier frequency in Hz. Range: 0–sampleRate/2. Should be significantly higher than the modulating signal frequency (typically 5–10+ times).

modulationIndex.description: modulation index/depth. For AM: modulation depth (0–1, where 1 = 100%). Values > 1 mean overmodulation. For FM: frequency deviation in Hz. Typical values: 75 (FM radio), 5 (narrowband). For PM: phase modulation index in radians. Typical values: 0.5–π.

examples.title: FM modulation and spectral analysis
examples.description: Sine(200 Hz) → AMFMPMModulator(FM, carrier 5000, deviation 1000) → SpectrumAnalyzer The spectrum shows the 5 kHz carrier with sidebands, bandwidth ≈ 2·(1000+200) = 2400 Hz.

examples.title: AM demodulation (envelope detection)
examples.description: Sine(300 Hz) → AMFMPMModulator(AM, 10000, m=0.5) → → AmplitudeDetector → LowpassFIR → Oscilloscope The envelope detector recovers the original 300 Hz signal.

examples.title: FM demodulation
examples.description: Sine(100 Hz) → AMFMPMModulator(FM, 8000, deviation 500) → → FrequencyDiscriminator → LowpassFIR → Oscilloscope The frequency discriminator extracts the modulating signal from FM.

psk-modulator.title: PSK Modulator
psk-modulator.purpose: Generates a Phase Shift Keying (PSK) modulated signal. PSK is the primary type of digital modulation where information is encoded in the carrier's phase. Each symbol corresponds to a specific point on the phase diagram (constellation). The block generates pseudo-random data via PRBS and produces I/Q samples.
psk-modulator.algorithm: 1. samplesPerSymbol = sampleRate / symbolRate is computed — the number of samples per symbol. For example, at sampleRate=48000 and symbolRate=1000, this gives 48. 2. When the sample counter reaches samplesPerSymbol, a new symbol is generated: - LFSR (Linear Feedback Shift Register) with polynomial 0x80000057 generates a pseudo-random bit sequence (PRBS). The LFSR is initialized with seed value 0x1234ABCD and provides a long uncorrelated sequence (period 2³² − 1). - From 1/2/3 bits (depending on the scheme), a constellation point (I, Q) is formed. 3. Between symbol changes, I/Q values remain constant (rectangular pulses — no pulse shaping).
psk-modulator.inputDescription: none (data is generated by internal PRBS)
psk-modulator.outputDescription: complex (interleaved Float32Array of length chunkSize × 2, [I0, Q0, I1, Q1, ...])

symbolRate.description: symbol rate in symbols/s (baud). Determines how many symbols are transmitted per second. Must be significantly less than sampleRate. Range: 10–sampleRate/4. Typical values: 100, 1000, 4800.

examples.title: Full QPSK demodulation chain
examples.description: PSKModulator(QPSK, sps=4) → noisy channel → → TimingRecovery(sps=4) → PLL → Constellation Symbol synchronization and PLL compensate for offsets; 4 clear points are visible on the constellation.

examples.title: PSK signal spectrum
examples.description: PSKModulator(BPSK, symbolRate 500) → SpectrumAnalyzer The spectrum has a sinc² shape with nulls at multiples of symbolRate from center. The main lobe occupies a bandwidth of 2 · symbolRate = 1000 Hz.

examples.title: Comparing modulation schemes
examples.description: PSKModulator(BPSK) → Constellation  (2 points on the I axis) PSKModulator(QPSK) → Constellation  (4 points at corners) PSKModulator(8PSK) → Constellation  (8 points on a circle)

notch-fir-filter.title: Notch FIR Filter
notch-fir-filter.purpose: Removes (suppresses) the signal in a narrow band around a specified frequency, passing all other frequencies unchanged. This is the opposite of a bandpass filter: a bandpass passes only the desired band, while a notch removes an unwanted one. Typical application — removing interference at a known frequency (50/60 Hz mains hum, tonal interference, pilot tone, etc.).
notch-fir-filter.algorithm: The filter is built using spectral inversion: first a bandpass FIR filter (windowed sinc) is designed for the target band, then its coefficients are inverted using the formula notch[n] = δ[n-center] - bandpass[n]. The result is a filter that subtracts the bandpass component from the signal. For precise rejection, the bandpass filter is normalized so that its gain at the center frequency equals 1.0. The filter order is forced to be odd (Type I linear phase) for integer group delay.
notch-fir-filter.outputDescription: real (Float32Array) — signal with the rejected band suppressed

notchFrequency.description: center rejection frequency in Hz. This frequency will be maximally suppressed. Valid range: 1 .. sampleRate/2 - 1.

bandwidth.description: rejection bandwidth in Hz. Determines how wide an area around notchFrequency will be suppressed. Narrow bandwidth (50–100 Hz) — pinpoint tone removal, wide (500+ Hz) — removal of an entire range.

order.description: filter order (number of coefficients). Higher order → steeper slopes and deeper rejection, but increases delay and computational load. Recommended range: 31–255. Automatically rounded to an odd value.

windowFunction.description: window function. Options: 'rectangular', 'hamming', 'hanning', 'blackman', 'blackman-harris', 'nuttall', 'flattop'. The window affects transition bandwidth and sidelobe level. Hamming is a good compromise, Blackman provides deeper sidelobe suppression.

examples.title: Suppressing 50 Hz mains hum
examples.description: AudioFile → NotchFIR(50Hz, bw=10, order=127) → Speaker Narrow bandwidth and high order precisely remove the hum with minimal impact on the useful signal.

examples.title: Cascade of notch filters
examples.description: Signal → NotchFIR(1000Hz) → NotchFIR(2000Hz) → NotchFIR(3000Hz) → Oscilloscope Sequential removal of multiple discrete interferences.

bandpass-fir-filter.title: Bandpass FIR Filter
bandpass-fir-filter.purpose: Passes the signal only within a specified frequency range (from lowCutoff to highCutoff), suppressing everything below and above this band. The bandpass filter is one of the basic DSP tools: it allows extracting a useful signal from a mixture, limiting bandwidth before demodulation, separating channels in a multi-channel system, etc.
bandpass-fir-filter.algorithm: Uses the windowed sinc filter method. The bandpass filter is constructed as the difference of two LPFs: one with cutoff frequency highCutoff, the other with lowCutoff. The coefficients are multiplied by the selected window function to control sidelobe levels. Implementation via createFIRProcessor('bandpass') factory from FIRFilterPlugin.
bandpass-fir-filter.outputDescription: real (Float32Array) — signal containing only the [lowCutoff, highCutoff] band

order.description: filter order (number of coefficients). Higher order → steeper passband slopes, but increases delay. Recommended range: 16–512.

lowCutoff.description: lower passband boundary in Hz. Frequencies below this value are suppressed.

highCutoff.description: upper passband boundary in Hz. Frequencies above this value are suppressed. Must satisfy: lowCutoff < highCutoff < sampleRate/2.

examples.title: Filtering before demodulation
examples.description: Sine(2000) + NoiseGenerator → Summer → BandpassFIR(1500–2500Hz) → Oscilloscope The bandpass filter extracts the 2 kHz signal from noise.

examples.title: In-band spectrum analysis
examples.description: AudioFile → BandpassFIR(1000–3000Hz) → SpectrumAnalyzer Only components in the 1–3 kHz band are visible on the spectrum analyzer.

highpass-fir-filter.title: Highpass FIR Filter
highpass-fir-filter.purpose: Passes frequencies above a specified cutoff frequency, suppressing all low-frequency components. HPF is used for removing DC offset, low-frequency drift, infrasonic interference, and extracting high-frequency signal components.
highpass-fir-filter.algorithm: Built on the windowed sinc filter method using spectral inversion of an LPF: first an LPF with cutoff frequency is designed, then its coefficients are inverted to obtain an HPF. Implementation via createFIRProcessor('highpass') factory from FIRFilterPlugin.

order.description: filter order (number of coefficients). Higher order → steeper slope at the cutoff frequency. Recommended range: 16–512. Small values (16–32) give a gradual transition, large values (128–512) give a nearly ideal brick-wall slope.

cutoff.description: cutoff frequency in Hz. Frequencies below cutoff are suppressed, above — pass unchanged. Valid range: 1 .. sampleRate/2 - 1.

examples.title: Extracting high-frequency noise
examples.description: AudioFile → HighpassFIR(5000Hz, order=128) → SpectrumAnalyzer Only components above 5 kHz are visible on the spectrum.

examples.title: HPF + LPF cascade = bandpass filter
examples.description: Signal → HighpassFIR(1000Hz) → LowpassFIR(3000Hz) → Oscilloscope Equivalent to a 1–3 kHz bandpass filter (but less efficient than a dedicated BandpassFIR).

lowpass-fir-filter.title: Lowpass FIR Filter
lowpass-fir-filter.purpose: Passes frequencies below a specified cutoff frequency, suppressing high-frequency components. LPF is the most common filter type in DSP. Used for signal smoothing, high-frequency noise removal, anti-aliasing filtering before decimation, bandwidth limiting, and envelope extraction.
lowpass-fir-filter.algorithm: Uses the windowed sinc filter method. The ideal LPF has an impulse response of the form sinc(2*fc*n), which is infinite. Truncation to a finite number of samples (order) and multiplication by a window function yields a practically realizable filter with controllable sidelobe levels. Implementation via createFIRProcessor('lowpass') factory from FIRFilterPlugin.
lowpass-fir-filter.outputDescription: real (Float32Array) — smoothed signal without high-frequency components

order.description: filter order (number of coefficients). Higher order → steeper slope and better suppression, but increases delay by order/2 samples. Recommended range: 16–512.

cutoff.description: cutoff frequency in Hz. Frequencies below cutoff pass through, above are suppressed. Valid range: 1 .. sampleRate/2 - 1.

windowFunction.description: window function. Options: 'rectangular', 'hamming', 'hanning', 'blackman', 'blackman-harris', 'nuttall', 'flattop'. Hamming provides ~43 dB sidelobe suppression, Blackman ~58 dB, Blackman-Harris ~92 dB.

examples.title: Anti-aliasing filter before decimation
examples.description: AudioFile → LowpassFIR(4000Hz, order=128) → DecimatorInterpolator(factor=4) The LPF limits bandwidth to 4 kHz before downsampling by 4, preventing aliasing.

examples.title: AM signal envelope extraction
examples.description: AMFMPMModulator(AM) → AmplitudeDetector → LowpassFIR(100Hz) → Oscilloscope The LPF smooths the envelope, removing carrier frequency remnants.

hilbert-transformer.title: Hilbert Transformer
hilbert-transformer.purpose: Converts a real signal into a complex (analytic) signal. The analytic signal is a complex signal of the form z(t) = x(t) + j*H{x(t)}, where x(t) is the original signal and H{x(t)} is its Hilbert transform (phase shift of all frequency components by 90°). The analytic signal has no negative frequencies in its spectrum, which simplifies extraction of instantaneous amplitude, frequency, and phase. In simple terms: if the input is a sinusoid cos(wt), the output will be a complex exponential cos(wt) + j*sin(wt), from which amplitude (magnitude) and phase (argument) are easily obtained.
hilbert-transformer.algorithm: Implemented as an FIR filter with Hilbert transform coefficients: h[n] = 2/(π*n) for odd n, h[n] = 0 for even n and n = 0. Coefficients are multiplied by a Blackman window for sidelobe suppression. Order is forced to be odd. - Q component (imaginary part): result of convolving the input with Hilbert coefficients — the signal shifted by 90°. - I component (real part): the original input delayed by (N-1)/2 samples to compensate for the filter's group delay.

order.description: Hilbert filter order. Higher order → more accurate transform at low frequencies, but increases delay. Automatically rounded to odd. Recommended range: 31–255.

phaseShift.description: phase shift in degrees. The standard value of 90° corresponds to the classical Hilbert transform. Reserved for future extensions.

examples.title: Extracting instantaneous phase
examples.description: Sine(1000) → HilbertTransformer → ComplexPhase → Oscilloscope A linearly increasing (sawtooth) phase is visible on the oscilloscope, corresponding to a 1 kHz frequency.

examples.title: AM signal envelope
examples.description: AMFMPMModulator(AM, carrier=5000Hz) → HilbertTransformer → → ComplexMagnitude → LowpassFIR(100Hz) → Oscilloscope The magnitude of the analytic signal = instantaneous amplitude (envelope).

goertzel-filter.title: Goertzel Filter
goertzel-filter.purpose: Computes the power (magnitude) of a signal at a single specified frequency. This is analogous to a single DFT/FFT bin, but significantly more efficient when only one or two frequencies need to be analyzed rather than the full spectrum. Classic applications: DTMF tone detection, pilot tone presence detection, signal level measurement at a specific frequency, simple frequency analysis.
goertzel-filter.algorithm: The Goertzel algorithm is a recursive method for computing a single DFT element. Instead of computing all N frequency bins (as in FFT), only one is calculated. At each sample, two states s1 and s2 are updated: s0 = x[n] + coeff * s1 - s2, where coeff = 2*cos(2π*k/N) After accumulating N samples, the result is computed: Re = s1 - s2*cos(2π*k/N), Im = s2*sin(2π*k/N) magnitude = sqrt(Re² + Im²) / (N/2) Then the states are reset and a new block begins. Computational complexity: O(N) per block for one frequency, whereas FFT would require O(N*log(N)) for all frequencies.
goertzel-filter.outputDescription: real (Float32Array) — magnitude at the target frequency (updated every N samples)

targetFrequency.description: analysis frequency in Hz. Power is measured at exactly this frequency. Valid range: 0 .. sampleRate/2.

N.description: analysis block size (number of samples per computation). Determines frequency resolution: Δf = sampleRate / N. For example, at sampleRate=48000 and N=256, resolution = 187.5 Hz. Larger N → better resolution but slower updates. Recommended range: 64–4096.

examples.title: Signal presence detection
examples.description: AudioFile → Goertzel(440Hz, N=1024) → Threshold(0.1) → NumericIndicator Detects whether the note A4 (440 Hz) is present in the signal.

examples.title: Comparison with full spectrum
examples.description: Sine(1000) → Goertzel(1000Hz) → Oscilloscope  (fast, single frequency) Sine(1000) → SpectrumAnalyzer                  (slower, full spectrum) Goertzel is more efficient when only one frequency is of interest.

remez-filter.title: Remez Filter
remez-filter.purpose: A bandpass filter designed using the Remez (Parks-McClellan) algorithm. Unlike the windowed sinc method (BandpassFIR), the Remez algorithm minimizes the maximum error (equiripple design): ripples in the passband and stopband are uniformly distributed and have equal amplitude. This yields an optimal filter for a given order — steeper slopes and better suppression than the windowed method with the same number of coefficients.
remez-filter.algorithm: The Parks-McClellan (Remez exchange) algorithm is an iterative method for designing FIR filters with linear phase. At each iteration: 1. Extrema (points of maximum error) are found in the frequency response. 2. Coefficients are recalculated to make the error uniform. 3. The process repeats until convergence. Order is forced to be odd (Type I linear phase). Advantages over windowed sinc: for the same filter order, Remez provides steeper slopes and deeper suppression. Disadvantage: design is slower (iterative algorithm).
remez-filter.outputDescription: real (Float32Array) — filtered signal within the specified band

order.description: filter order. Automatically rounded to odd. Higher order → steeper slopes. Recommended range: 31–501. Coefficient computation at high orders may take noticeable time.

examples.title: Comparison with windowed filter
examples.description: Signal → BandpassFIR(1000–3000Hz, order=64)  → SpectrumAnalyzer Signal → Remez(1000–3000Hz, order=64)         → SpectrumAnalyzer At the same order, Remez shows better out-of-band suppression.

examples.title: Speech filtering in a noisy channel
examples.description: AudioFile + NoiseGenerator → Summer → Remez(300–3400Hz, order=151) → Speaker The optimal filter maximally suppresses noise outside the speech range.

delay-line.title: Delay Line
delay-line.purpose: Delays the input signal by a specified number of samples. The delay line is a fundamental building block in DSP: used in comb filters, echo effects, group delay compensation of other filters, correlation analysis, and many other tasks. Before the buffer fills (first N samples), the output is zeros.
delay-line.algorithm: Implemented via a circular buffer of size N. At each sample: the value at the current buffer position is read (this is the delayed signal), then the new input sample is written to the same position, and the pointer advances around the ring. This provides exactly N samples of delay with O(1) per sample. When the delay length changes during operation, the buffer is recreated with the tail of the old buffer copied — this prevents clicks and discontinuities in the signal.
delay-line.outputDescription: real (Float32Array) — delayed copy of the input signal

delaySamples.description: number of delay samples. Delay in seconds = delaySamples / sampleRate. For example, at sampleRate=48000: 100 samples ≈ 2.08 ms, 48000 samples = 1 second. Valid range: 0 .. ∞ (at 0 the signal passes unchanged).

examples.title: Compensating filter delay
examples.description: Signal ─┬─→ LowpassFIR(order=64) → Summer → Oscilloscope └─→ DelayLine(32)        ──↗ A delay of 32 samples compensates the group delay of a 64th-order LPF (order/2), allowing correct subtraction of the filtered signal.

examples.title: Correlation analysis
examples.description: Signal → DelayLine(N) → Correlator(with original) Autocorrelation with delay N allows detecting periodicities.

decimator-interpolator.title: Decimation/Interpolation
decimator-interpolator.purpose: Changes the signal's sample rate: decreases (decimation) or increases (interpolation) the number of samples. This is necessary when different parts of the system operate at different sample rates, or when computational load needs to be reduced by processing fewer samples per second. Decimation: reducing the sample rate by a factor (e.g., 48000 Hz → 12000 Hz at factor=4). An anti-aliasing LPF is applied before downsampling to prevent spectral folding. Interpolation: increasing the sample rate by a factor. Zeros are inserted between existing samples (zero-stuffing), then an anti-imaging LPF is applied for smoothing.
decimator-interpolator.algorithm: Decimation: 1. If filterEnabled, the input signal is filtered by an LPF with cutoff Fs/(2*factor) to prevent aliasing. 2. Every factor-th sample is taken from the filtered signal. Interpolation: 1. Between samples, (factor-1) zeros are inserted, amplitude is multiplied by factor to compensate for gain. 2. If filterEnabled, an LPF with cutoff Fs/(2*factor) is applied to suppress spectral images. The internal LPF is implemented as a sinc filter with Hamming window; filter length adapts to the decimation/interpolation factor.

mode.description: operating mode: 'decimate' — downsampling (reducing sample rate), 'interpolate' — upsampling (increasing sample rate).

factor.description: rate change factor. For decimation: output rate = input / factor. For interpolation: output rate = input * factor. Valid range: 1–16.

filterEnabled.description: enable/disable the built-in anti-aliasing/anti-imaging filter. Disabling is useful if the signal is already filtered by an external filter (e.g., a higher-quality LowpassFIR).

examples.title: Upsampling before DAC
examples.description: Signal(12kHz) → DecimatorInterpolator(interpolate, factor=4) → Speaker Rate increased to 48 kHz for output through the sound card.

examples.title: Multi-stage decimation
examples.description: Signal → DecimatorInterpolator(decimate, 4) → DecimatorInterpolator(decimate, 4) Two-stage decimation by 16 — more efficient than single-stage with factor=16, as the intermediate LPF operates at a lower rate.

cic-filter.title: CIC Filter
cic-filter.purpose: Cascaded Integrator-Comb — a specialized filter for sample rate conversion (decimation or interpolation). The main advantage of CIC is the absence of multiplication operations: the filter consists only of adders and delay elements. This makes it extremely efficient at large decimation factors (10x and more), where conventional FIR filters would require too many computations. CIC filters are widely used in SDR receivers (Software Defined Radio) at the first processing stage to reduce the ADC sample rate (e.g., from 100 MHz to 1 MHz).
cic-filter.algorithm: Filter structure: a cascade of N integrators → rate change → cascade of N combs, where N = stages (number of cascades). Decimation: 1. Each input sample passes through the integrator cascade: y[n] = y[n-1] + x[n] (cumulative sum). 2. Every R-th sample (R = decimationFactor) is passed to the comb cascade: y[n] = x[n] - x[n-1] (first difference). 3. Remaining samples are discarded (downsampling). Interpolation (reverse order): 1. Input passes through combs. 2. R-1 zeros are inserted between samples (zero-stuffing). 3. The expanded signal passes through integrators. The CIC frequency response is sinc^N(f), meaning non-uniform suppression in the stopband. A compensating FIR filter (CIC compensation filter) is typically placed after the CIC. To prevent integer overflow during prolonged operation, integrators are implemented on Int32Array with modular (wrapping) arithmetic. Float → int32 scaling: ×32768.
cic-filter.outputDescription: real (Float32Array) — signal with changed sample rate

stages.description: number of cascades (integrators and combs). More stages → steeper filter slope (suppression ~stages × 20 dB at Nyquist), but more passband droop. Valid range: 1–6.

mode.description: operating mode: 'decimate' — reduce sample rate by R times, 'interpolate' — increase sample rate by R times.

examples.title: Comparison with standard decimation
examples.description: Signal → CIC(stages=3, R=4)                 → Oscilloscope  (no multiplications) Signal → DecimatorInterpolator(decimate, 4)  → Oscilloscope  (with FIR filter) CIC is faster at large R but has non-uniform frequency response.

examples.title: Interpolation
examples.description: Signal(12kHz) → CIC(stages=3, R=4, interpolate) → LowpassFIR → Speaker Rate increased by 4x. LPF after CIC removes residual spectral images and compensates for sinc droop.

iir-filter.title: IIR Filter
iir-filter.purpose: Implements digital filters with feedback (recursive). Unlike FIR filters, whose output depends only on input samples, an IIR filter also uses its own previous output values. This allows the IIR filter to achieve significantly steeper slopes at low orders: a 4th-order Butterworth filter gives an 80 dB/decade slope, whereas an FIR filter would require hundreds of coefficients for similar suppression. The disadvantage of IIR compared to FIR: nonlinear phase response — different frequencies are delayed by different amounts, which can distort the signal waveform. If linear phase is critical (e.g., in audio), FIR filters (LowpassFIR, HighpassFIR, etc.) are preferred.
iir-filter.algorithm: Two classic analog filter prototype designs are supported: Butterworth: Maximally flat magnitude response in the passband — no ripple. Slope: order × 20 dB/decade. Optimal choice for most tasks. Chebyshev Type I: Steeper slope than Butterworth at the same order, but at the cost of equiripple in the passband. The ripple parameter (dB) sets the allowable ripple amplitude. The analog prototype is converted to a digital filter using the bilinear transform with frequency prewarping for accurate cutoff frequency matching. Implementation — cascade of biquad sections (Second-Order Sections / SOS). Each section is a 2nd-order filter with 5 coefficients (b0, b1, b2, a1, a2). Cascading ensures numerical stability even at high orders. HPF is designed via direct prototype transformation (s → ωc/s).

filterDesign.description: filter type: 'butterworth' — maximally flat magnitude response, 'chebyshev1' — steeper slope with passband ripple.

filterType.description: filter mode: 'lowpass' — LPF (passes low, suppresses high), 'highpass' — HPF (passes high, suppresses low).

cutoffFrequency.description: cutoff frequency in Hz. At this frequency the gain = -3 dB (Butterworth) or = -ripple dB (Chebyshev). Range: 1 .. sampleRate/2 - 1.

order.description: filter order. Determines slope steepness and number of biquad sections (ceil(order/2)). Valid range: 1–10. Orders above 8 may introduce numerical artifacts.

ripple.description: passband ripple amplitude in dB (Chebyshev Type I only). Smaller values (0.1–0.5) — minimal ripple but less steep slope. Larger values (1–3) — steep slope but noticeable ripple. Ignored for Butterworth.

examples.title: Comparing Butterworth and Chebyshev
examples.description: Signal → IIR(butterworth, lowpass, 1000Hz, order=4) → SpectrumAnalyzer Signal → IIR(chebyshev1, lowpass, 1000Hz, order=4, ripple=1) → SpectrumAnalyzer Chebyshev shows a steeper slope but with ±1 dB ripple in the 0–1000 Hz band.

examples.title: HPF for DC removal
examples.description: AudioFile → IIRFilter(butterworth, highpass, 20Hz, order=2) → Speaker A gentle 2nd-order HPF removes DC and infrasound with minimal impact on the audio signal.

spectrum-analyzer.title: Spectrum Analyzer
spectrum-analyzer.purpose: Shows the frequency content of the input signal in real time. Any signal can be represented as a sum of sinusoids of different frequencies and amplitudes — the spectrum analyzer decomposes the signal into these components and displays them as an 'amplitude vs. frequency' graph. This is the primary diagnostic tool in digital signal processing: it allows seeing the useful signal, noise, harmonics, interference, and evaluating filtering effectiveness.
spectrum-analyzer.algorithm: 1. Input samples are written into a circular buffer of size fftSize. 2. On each process() call, the buffer contents are copied and multiplied by a window function (Blackman-Harris by default). The window smooths the data block edges, reducing spectral leakage. 3. A Fast Fourier Transform (FFT) is performed, converting the time-domain signal to the frequency domain. 4. The magnitude (amplitude) of each frequency component is computed from the complex FFT coefficients — in decibels (dB) or linear scale. 5. Exponential averaging is applied: S[n] = S[n-1] + α·(X[n] - S[n-1]), where α = 1/averaging. Averaging smooths noise peaks on the spectrum at the cost of slower response to signal changes.
spectrum-analyzer.outputDescription: null (visualization block, data is passed to SpectrumView)

fftSize.description: FFT size, determines frequency resolution: Δf = sampleRate / fftSize. Must be a power of two. Typical values: 512, 1024, 2048, 4096, 8192. Larger → more accurate in frequency but slower updates.

windowFunction.description: window function. Options: 'hann', 'hamming', 'blackman', 'blackman-harris', 'rectangular'. Blackman-Harris provides the best sidelobe suppression (-92 dB) but slightly widens the main lobe.

dBScale.description: display in decibels. In dB it is more convenient: a 60–100 dB dynamic range is visible on a single graph. In linear scale, weak signals are practically indistinguishable.

averaging.description: number of exponential averaging frames. 1 = no averaging (maximum time resolution). 5–10 = smoothed spectrum (convenient for noise level estimation). 20+ = heavy averaging (for stationary signals).

examples.title: Evaluating filtering
examples.description: NoiseGenerator → LowpassFIR(cutoff=2000) → SpectrumAnalyzer The noise spectrum is cut off above 2 kHz — the characteristic filter frequency response slope is visible. Slope steepness depends on filter order.

examples.title: Finding harmonics
examples.description: AudioFile → SpectrumAnalyzer(fftSize=4096, averaging=10) Increased FFT size and averaging reveal fine spectral structure: fundamental tone, overtones, artifacts.

correlator.title: Correlator
correlator.purpose: Cross-correlation is a measure of similarity between two signals as a function of time shift (lag) between them. Imagine 'sliding' one signal along the other and at each step computing how similar they are. The correlation function peak indicates the lag at which the signals best match. Typical applications: - Time delay estimation: if one signal is a delayed copy of the other, the correlation peak shows the delay magnitude. - Signal detection in noise: correlation with a reference signal (matched filter) extracts the useful signal even at low signal-to-noise ratio. - Similarity measurement: the normalized correlation coefficient shows the degree of linear dependence between signals (from -1 to +1).
correlator.algorithm: Uses the fast FFT-based method: R(τ) = IFFT(FFT(x₁) · conj(FFT(x₂))), giving O(N·log N) complexity instead of O(N²) for direct computation. Steps: 1. If normalization is enabled, mean values of both signals are subtracted and their energies are calculated for subsequent division. 2. Signals are zero-padded to the nearest power of two for correct linear (not circular) correlation. 3. FFT(x₁) and FFT(x₂) are computed, then element-wise product FFT(x₁) · conj(FFT(x₂)), then inverse FFT. 4. The result is normalized: divided by sqrt(E₁ · E₂), where E is signal energy. 5. The output array is centered: lag 0 is in the middle, negative lags on the left, positive on the right.
correlator.outputDescription: real (Float32Array — correlation function, lag 0 at the center of the array)

normalize.description: correlation normalization. When enabled: means are subtracted (DC removed), result is divided by sqrt(E₁·E₂). Output values range [-1, +1], where +1 means perfect match, 0 means no relationship, -1 means anti-phase. When disabled: output is 'raw' correlation (product of amplitudes).

maxLag.description: maximum lag for computation. 0 = full range (all lags from -chunkSize/2 to +chunkSize/2). Limiting the lag speeds up processing if the delay is known not to exceed a certain value.

examples.title: Signal detection in noise
examples.description: [Sine(1000) + NoiseGenerator(level=2)] → Correlator (Input 1) Sine(1000) → Correlator (Input 2, reference) → Oscilloscope Even with strong noise, correlation with a clean reference produces a pronounced peak.

examples.title: Comparing two different signals
examples.description: Sine(1000) → Correlator (Input 1) Sine(2000) → Correlator (Input 2) → NumericIndicator Normalized correlation is close to 0 — signals of different frequencies do not correlate.

phase-detector.title: Phase Detector
phase-detector.purpose: Extracts the instantaneous phase from a complex (I/Q) signal and presents it in one of several formats. Phase is the angle of the (I, Q) vector on the complex plane. For a sinusoid with constant frequency, the phase increases linearly over time (sawtooth shape in the periodic range, linear growth when accumulated). For a phase-modulated signal, the phase contains the information signal.
phase-detector.algorithm: 1. From complex sample z[n] = I + jQ, instantaneous phase is computed: φ[n] = atan2(Q, I), result in range (−π, π]. 2. Phase unwrapping: Δφ = φ[n] − φ[n−1] is computed, and if |Δφ| > π, it is corrected by ±2π. This eliminates discontinuities at ±π transitions. 3. Accumulation: accumPhase += Δφ. Accumulated phase grows (or decreases) continuously without jumps. 4. Conversion to the selected output format (outputRange). 5. Scaling by the sensitivity coefficient. Protection: when magnitude |z| < 1e-10, phase is undefined — the last accumulated value is output.
phase-detector.outputDescription: real (Float32Array) — phase in the selected format × sensitivity

referenceFrequency.description: reference frequency. In the current implementation, used for informational purposes. Recommended range: 0–sampleRate/2.

sensitivity.description: output gain coefficient. Scales the phase value. Values > 1 amplify, < 1 attenuate. Recommended range: 0.01–100.

outputRange.description: output value format: '±180°' — accumulated phase in degrees (continuous growth/decrease). For a 1 kHz sinusoid at sampleRate=48000, phase grows by 7.5° per sample (360°·1000/48000). '0-360°' — phase in degrees, wrapped to [0, 360). Sawtooth shape with period equal to the signal period. '0-2π' — phase in radians, wrapped to [0, 2π). Same as '0-360°' but in radians. '±π' — accumulated phase in radians (continuous growth/decrease). The most 'raw' format, convenient for further processing.

examples.title: Sawtooth phase
examples.description: RefSine(1000) → ComplexComposer → PhaseDetector(0-360°) → Oscilloscope Phase 'wraps' every 360°, creating a sawtooth shape with 1000 Hz repetition rate.

examples.title: Phase modulation demodulation
examples.description: AMFMPMModulator(PM) → HilbertTransformer → PhaseDetector(±π, sens=1.0) → Oscilloscope Extracted phase follows the modulating signal shape. '±π' mode is convenient for PM demodulation since the output in radians directly corresponds to the modulation index.

examples.title: Phase shift measurement
examples.description: RefSine(1000) → ComplexComposer → PhaseDetector(±180°) → NumericIndicator Current phase value on the indicator. Useful for calibration and comparing phase delays between blocks.

frequency-detector.title: Frequency Detector
frequency-detector.purpose: Determines the instantaneous frequency of a complex signal and extracts only components falling within a specified passband around the center frequency. This is useful when tracking the frequency of a specific spectral component in a signal while ignoring noise and interference outside the band.
frequency-detector.algorithm: 1. From complex sample z[n] = I + jQ, phase is extracted: φ[n] = atan2(Q, I) 2. Phase difference with unwrapping: Δφ = unwrap(φ[n] − φ[n−1]) The unwrapPhaseDelta function corrects phase jumps through ±π. 3. Instantaneous frequency: f = Δφ · sampleRate / (2π) [Hz] 4. Deviation from center: deviation = f − centerFrequency 5. Band filtering: if |deviation| > bandwidth/2, output = 0. This is equivalent to a hard (rectangular) frequency window. 6. Result is scaled by the sensitivity coefficient: out = deviation × sensitivity Protection against division by zero: when magnitude |z| < 1e-10, output is zeroed.
frequency-detector.outputDescription: real (Float32Array) — frequency deviation from center (Hz × sensitivity)

centerFrequency.description: detector center frequency. Output shows deviation from this value. Recommended range: 0–sampleRate/2.

bandwidth.description: passband width. Samples with deviation greater than bandwidth/2 are zeroed. Narrow bandwidth (10–50 Hz) — precise tracking of a single frequency. Wide bandwidth (200–1000 Hz) — allows larger deviation. Recommended range: 1–10000 Hz.

sensitivity.description: output gain coefficient. Scales the deviation value. Values > 1 amplify, < 1 attenuate the output signal. Recommended range: 0.01–100. Difference from FrequencyDiscriminator: FrequencyDiscriminator outputs 'raw' instantaneous frequency without filtering — useful for wideband analysis. FrequencyDetector adds band filtering and scaling — useful for tracking a specific frequency in a noisy signal.

examples.title: Narrowband FM detection
examples.description: AMFMPMModulator(FM, fc=1000, dev=30) → HilbertTransformer → FrequencyDetector(fc=1000, BW=100, sens=1.0) → Oscilloscope The detector passes ±30 Hz deviation (within the ±50 Hz band). The oscilloscope shows the recovered modulating signal.

examples.title: Selective measurement
examples.description: [signal with multiple tones] → FrequencyDetector(fc=500, BW=50) → NumericIndicator The detector responds only to the component near 500 Hz, ignoring other frequencies.

amplitude-detector.title: Amplitude Detector
amplitude-detector.purpose: Extracts the amplitude envelope of the input signal. The envelope is a smooth curve describing signal amplitude changes over time. For example, for a guitar string sound, the envelope shows a fast attack and slow decay. This block operates similarly to a level detector in analog compressors and limiters.
amplitude-detector.algorithm: Uses exponential smoothing with separate time constants for rise (attack) and fall (release): if |x[n]| > env[n-1]: env[n] = env[n-1] + αₐ · (|x[n]| − env[n-1])   // attack (fast) else: env[n] = env[n-1] + αᵣ · (|x[n]| − env[n-1])   // release (slow) where smoothing coefficients: αₐ = 1 − exp(−1 / (sampleRate · attackTime_sec)) αᵣ = 1 − exp(−1 / (sampleRate · releaseTime_sec)) Fast attack allows instant tracking of signal peaks, while slow release provides smooth envelope decay without chatter.

attackTime.description: attack time (rise). Determines how quickly the detector responds to amplitude increases. Small values (0.1–1 ms) → instant reaction to peaks. Large values (5–20 ms) → smoothed response. Recommended range: 0.01–50 ms.

releaseTime.description: release time (decay). Determines how quickly the envelope decays after amplitude decreases. Small values (10–30 ms) → envelope closely follows the signal. Large values (100–500 ms) → smooth, 'lazy' envelope. Recommended range: 1–1000 ms.

examples.title: AM detection
examples.description: AMFMPMModulator(AM) → AmplitudeDetector(attack=0.1, release=10) → Oscilloscope Fast envelope detector recovers the modulating signal from the AM waveform (alternative to AMFMPMDemodulator for simple cases).

examples.title: Signal level measurement
examples.description: Sine(1000) → AmplitudeDetector(attack=5, release=200) → NumericIndicator Slow detector shows the average signal level on the indicator.

pll.title: PLL
pll.purpose: Phase error extraction via atan2(Q·I_nco - I·Q_nco, I·I_nco + Q·Q_nco) 2. Loop filter — proportional-integral (PI) controller: u(n) = Kp·e(n) + Ki·∑e(k) where Kp and Ki are calculated from the natural frequency ωn and damping coefficient ζ using Gardner's formulas: Kp = 2·ζ·ωn, Ki = ωn² 3. NCO (Numerically Controlled Oscillator) — phase accumulator controlled by the sum of base frequency and loop filter output
pll.algorithm: 1. Phase detector — multiplication of the input signal with the reference NCO, phase error extraction via atan2(Q·I_nco - I·Q_nco, I·I_nco + Q·Q_nco) 2. Loop filter — proportional-integral (PI) controller: u(n) = Kp·e(n) + Ki·∑e(k) where Kp and Ki are calculated from the natural frequency ωn and damping coefficient ζ using Gardner's formulas: Kp = 2·ζ·ωn, Ki = ωn² 3. NCO (Numerically Controlled Oscillator) — phase accumulator controlled by the sum of base frequency and loop filter output
pll.outputDescription: complex — NCO output (recovered carrier, interleaved I/Q)

examples.title: Carrier recovery in a PSK receiver
examples.description: PSKModulator(QPSK, sps=4) → TimingRecovery(sps=4) → PLL(fc=0, BW=30) → Constellation In the digital receiver chain, PLL compensates for carrier phase offset. Without PLL, QPSK constellation points are rotated by an arbitrary angle; after PLL they are aligned to axes. centerFrequency = 0 because the signal after TimingRecovery is already at zero intermediate frequency.

examples.title: Loop acquisition analysis
examples.description: RefSine(1050) → ComplexComposer → PLL(fc=1000, BW=100) → [output 1: phase error] → Oscilloscope Initial frequency offset of 50 Hz. The oscilloscope shows how the phase error oscillates initially and decays to zero as the loop acquires lock. Bandwidth BW=100 Hz is sufficient to capture a 50 Hz offset.

amfmpm-demodulator.title: AM/FM/PM Demodulator
amfmpm-demodulator.purpose: Extracts the information (modulating) signal from a modulated waveform. Supports three types of analog modulation: amplitude (AM), frequency (FM), and phase (PM). The input is a real signal; internally an analytic (complex) signal is formed via the Hilbert transform, after which the desired parameter is extracted.
amfmpm-demodulator.algorithm: Key idea — converting the real signal to analytic: z(t) = x(t) + j·H{x(t)}, where H{} is the Hilbert transform creating the quadrature (Q) component. The I component is the input delayed by HILBERT_M samples. A 31-tap FIR Hilbert filter with Hamming window is used. Demodulation modes: - AM (amplitude modulation): Envelope = |z(t)| = √(I² + Q²). Information is encoded in carrier amplitude. After envelope extraction, DC blocking is applied (filter: y[n] = x[n] - x[n-1] + 0.995·y[n-1]) to remove the DC component corresponding to the carrier level. - FM (frequency modulation): Instantaneous frequency = d(phase)/dt. Computed via the product conj(z[n-1])·z[n], where the phase difference = atan2(Im, Re) of this product. Result is scaled: f = Δφ · sampleRate / (2π). Information is encoded in frequency deviation from the carrier. - PM (phase modulation): Instantaneous phase = atan2(Q, I). Information is encoded directly in the carrier phase. Output values are in radians (from -π to π).

carrierFrequency.description: carrier frequency. Used for informational purposes (in the current implementation does not directly affect the algorithm, as the Hilbert filter operates wideband).

examples.title: AM signal demodulation
examples.description: AMFMPMModulator(AM) → AMFMPMDemodulator(AM) → Oscilloscope The envelope detector extracts the modulating signal from the AM waveform. DC blocking removes the carrier's DC component.

examples.title: PM signal phase analysis
examples.description: AMFMPMModulator(PM) → AMFMPMDemodulator(PM) → Oscilloscope Extracted phase follows the modulating signal shape.

examples.title: Spectral analysis after demodulation
examples.description: AMFMPMModulator(FM) → AMFMPMDemodulator(FM) → SpectrumAnalyzer Verifies that the demodulated signal spectrum matches the original modulating signal.

frequency-discriminator.title: Frequency Discriminator
frequency-discriminator.purpose: Computes the instantaneous frequency of a complex (analytic) signal by differentiating the phase. Unlike FrequencyDetector, this block outputs the 'raw' frequency value without band filtering, making it a universal tool for frequency analysis. Instantaneous frequency is the rate of phase change at a given moment. For a sinusoid with constant frequency, the instantaneous frequency is constant and equals the sinusoid's frequency. For an FM signal, it varies over time, following the modulating signal's shape.
frequency-discriminator.algorithm: 1. From complex sample z[n] = I + jQ, phase is extracted: φ[n] = atan2(Q, I) 2. Phase difference is computed: Δφ = φ[n] − φ[n−1] 3. Phase unwrapping is performed: if |Δφ| > π, correct by ±2π to avoid jumps at ±π transitions. 4. Instantaneous frequency: f = Δφ · sampleRate / (2π) [Hz] Protection against division by zero: when magnitude |z| < 1e-10, output is zeroed, as phase is undefined for a zero signal.
frequency-discriminator.outputDescription: real (Float32Array) — instantaneous frequency (Hz or deviation in Hz)

outputMode.description: output mode: 'deviation' — deviation from center frequency (f − centerFrequency). Convenient for FM analysis when only deviation is needed. 'absolute' — absolute instantaneous frequency in Hz. Convenient for general frequency analysis.

centerFrequency.description: center frequency subtracted in 'deviation' mode. Set the carrier frequency to get only deviation at the output. Recommended range: 0–sampleRate/2. Difference from FrequencyDetector: FrequencyDetector has band filtering (zeros output outside the specified bandwidth) and a sensitivity coefficient. FrequencyDiscriminator outputs an unfiltered frequency value — useful for wideband analysis and FM demodulation where the full deviation range is needed.

examples.title: Absolute frequency measurement
examples.description: RefSine(1000) → FrequencyDiscriminator(absolute) → NumericIndicator The indicator shows a value of ~1000 Hz (instantaneous frequency of the sinusoid).

examples.title: Frequency instability analysis
examples.description: RefSine(1000) → ComplexComposer → FrequencyDiscriminator(absolute) → Oscilloscope Allows observing generator frequency fluctuations on the oscilloscope.

timing-recovery.title: Timing Recovery
timing-recovery.purpose: Recovers optimal sampling instants in a digital receiver. The input is a stream of samples with oversampling (multiple samples per symbol); the output is one sample per symbol taken at the best moment in time. This is a key block in the demodulation chain, without which the phase constellation will be 'smeared'.
timing-recovery.algorithm: Uses the Gardner Timing Error Detector (TED) — a non-coherent synchronization error detector that does not require knowledge of the carrier frequency. Error formula: e = Re{(prev_symbol - current_symbol) * conj(midpoint)}, where midpoint is the sample halfway between two symbols. The error is fed to a PI loop filter (proportional-integral), which smoothly adjusts the sampling interval (symbol period).

samplesPerSymbol.description: number of samples per symbol in the input signal. Determined by modulator/channel parameters. Typical values: 2, 4, 8.

loopBandwidth.description: normalized synchronization loop bandwidth. Smaller values → slower acquisition but more precise tracking. Larger values → faster acquisition but more jitter. Recommended range: 0.001–0.05.

damping.description: loop damping coefficient. A value of 1/√2 ≈ 0.707 provides critical damping (optimal balance between speed and stability). Usually does not require adjustment.

examples.title: 8-PSK demodulation
examples.description: PSKModulator(8PSK, sps=8) → BandpassFIR → → TimingRecovery(sps=8, BW=0.005) → Constellation With more constellation points, reducing loopBandwidth is recommended to decrease sampling jitter.

examples.title: Synchronization quality analysis
examples.description: PSKModulator → TimingRecovery → Oscilloscope The oscilloscope shows that the output contains a decimated signal (sps times fewer samples) — one per symbol. Symbol amplitudes cluster around nominal values. Why complex signals: Digital modulation encodes information in two components — I (in-phase) and Q (quadrature). TimingRecovery operates on both simultaneously because the sampling instant must be the same for I and Q. The output is one complex sample (I+jQ) per symbol at the optimal time.

summer.title: Summer
summer.purpose: Adds two (or more) real signals with specified weight coefficients. This is one of the basic DSP blocks, necessary for mixing signals, forming sum/difference channels, and building feedback loops. In analog electronics, the equivalent is an operational amplifier in summing mode.
summer.algorithm: For each sample: y[n] = w0·x0[n] + w1·x1[n] + ... After summation, normalization may be applied: averaging (dividing by the number of active inputs) or peak normalization (dividing by the maximum absolute value of the output signal in the chunk).

numInputs.description: number of summer inputs. Determines how many signals can be connected simultaneously.

weights.description: weight coefficients for each input. A negative weight inverts the signal (subtraction). Array length must match numInputs.

normalization.description: normalization mode: 'none' — no normalization, output = weighted sum; 'average' — divide by number of active inputs (mean); 'peak' — peak normalization (maximum = 1.0).

examples.title: Signal subtraction (adaptive cancellation)
examples.description: Summer(weights: [1.0, -1.0]) — subtracts the second input from the first. Useful for interference suppression: original signal on the first input, interference estimate on the second.

examples.title: Channel averaging
examples.description: Summer(normalization: 'average') — average of two signals. Used for noise reduction when multiple measurements are available.

multiplier.title: Multiplier
multiplier.purpose: Multiplies (or divides) two real signals element-wise with an additional scale factor. In radio engineering, signal multiplication is the basis of amplitude modulation, balanced mixing, and synchronous detection. Multiplying two sinusoidal signals with frequencies f1 and f2 produces components at frequencies f1+f2 and f1-f2 in the spectrum (trigonometric product identity).
multiplier.algorithm: Multiplication: y[n] = x0[n] · x1[n] · ... · scaleFactor Division: y[n] = x0[n] / x1[n] / ... · scaleFactor Division by zero yields 0 (protection against NaN/Infinity).

operation.description: operation type: 'multiply' — element-wise multiplication; 'divide' — element-wise division (first input divided by the rest).

scaleFactor.description: scale factor applied to the result. Useful for gain compensation.

examples.title: Synchronous detection
examples.description: AM signal × Sine(carrier) → Multiplier → LowpassFIR → Oscilloscope Multiplication by the carrier frequency translates the useful signal to the low-frequency range; the LPF extracts the envelope.

examples.title: Controlled attenuator
examples.description: Signal × Control → Multiplier(scaleFactor: 0.5) One signal modulates the amplitude of another.

integrator.title: Integrator
integrator.purpose: Computes the cumulative sum (integral) of the input signal over time. In DSP, integrators are used to convert frequency to phase (e.g., in numerically controlled oscillators — NCO), to compute mean values, and in control systems (PID controllers). The trapezoidal method is used — more accurate than simple summation (rectangular method), as it accounts for linear signal changes between samples.
integrator.algorithm: Trapezoidal method: y[n] = y[n-1] + (x[n] + x[n-1]) · dt / 2, where dt = 1/sampleRate is the sampling period. When maxValue is reached, either reset or saturation (clamp) occurs, preventing numerical overflow during prolonged operation.

resetOnOverflow.description: overflow behavior: true — reset accumulator to 0 (sawtooth output); false — saturate at ±maxValue (output is clamped).

maxValue.description: overflow threshold. Determines the maximum absolute accumulator value. Should be adjusted based on input signal amplitude and sampleRate.

examples.title: Frequency to phase conversion
examples.description: Frequency signal → Integrator → phase input for cos/sin Used in NCO (numerically controlled oscillator) implementation.

examples.title: Signal smoothing
examples.description: Noisy signal → Integrator(maxValue: 10) → Oscilloscope Integration suppresses high-frequency noise (acts as an LPF).

real-part.title: Re (Real Part)
real-part.purpose: Extracts the real (in-phase, I) component of a complex signal. Converts a complex signal to real by discarding the imaginary part. For the complex exponential exp(j2πft), the real part is cos(2πft). This block is needed for transitioning from complex to real representation when outputting to an oscilloscope, to Speaker, or for feeding blocks that accept only real signals.
real-part.algorithm: output[n] = input[2n] (even elements of the interleaved array) Output array size = input / 2.

examples.title: Transition to real signal
examples.description: Complex filter → RealPart → Speaker A real signal is needed for playback through the speaker.

examples.title: Separate I/Q processing
examples.description: Signal → RealPart → Process_I → [Re] Signal → ImagPart → Process_Q → [Im] → ComplexComposer Allows applying different real filters to I and Q components, then reassembling the result.

imag-part.title: Im (Imaginary Part)
imag-part.purpose: Extracts the imaginary (quadrature, Q) component of a complex signal. Converts a complex signal to real by discarding the real part. For the complex exponential exp(j2πft), the imaginary part is sin(2πft). This block is paired with RealPart and is used for quadrature component analysis, Q-channel visualization, and separate I/Q signal component processing.
imag-part.algorithm: output[n] = input[2n + 1] (odd elements of the interleaved array) Output array size = input / 2.

examples.title: I/Q balance check
examples.description: Signal → RealPart → Oscilloscope (channel 1) Signal → ImagPart → Oscilloscope (channel 2) I and Q amplitudes should be equal for a balanced quadrature signal.

examples.title: Q-channel demodulation
examples.description: QPSK → ImagPart → Threshold → NumericIndicator Extracting bits from the quadrature channel of a QPSK signal (after timing and phase synchronization).

complex-multiplier.title: Complex Multiplier
complex-multiplier.purpose: Multiplies two complex signals element-wise. Complex multiplication adds phases and multiplies amplitudes: if z1 = A·exp(jφ1) and z2 = B·exp(jφ2), then z1·z2 = A·B·exp(j(φ1+φ2)). This is a fundamental operation for frequency conversion (mixing), phase rotation, correlation, and NCO (numerically controlled oscillator) operations.
complex-multiplier.algorithm: (a + jb) · (c + jd) = (ac - bd) + j(ad + bc) Re_out[n] = Re1[n]·Re2[n] - Im1[n]·Im2[n] Im_out[n] = Re1[n]·Im2[n] + Im1[n]·Re2[n]

examples.title: Phase rotation
examples.description: Signal × Constant(cos(φ)+j·sin(φ)) → ComplexMultiplier Rotates all constellation points by angle φ — used in PLL for phase offset compensation.

examples.title: Cross-correlation
examples.description: Signal_A × ComplexConjugate(Signal_B) → ComplexMultiplier → FFT The product z1·conj(z2) in the frequency domain is equivalent to cross-correlation in the time domain.

complex-summer.title: Complex Summer
complex-summer.purpose: Adds two complex signals element-wise: real parts are added separately, imaginary parts separately. This is the complex analog of the regular Summer. Used for combining I/Q signals, summing channels in multi-channel systems, and forming sum and difference patterns in antenna arrays.
complex-summer.algorithm: Re_out[n] = Re1[n] + Re2[n] Im_out[n] = Im1[n] + Im2[n] If one input is not connected, its contribution is zero.

examples.title: Adding noise to a signal
examples.description: Signal + Complex_noise → ComplexSummer → Constellation Modeling a noisy communication channel — constellation points are 'smeared' around nominal positions.

examples.title: Sum channel formation
examples.description: Antenna_1 + Antenna_2 → ComplexSummer → Demodulator Coherent combining of signals from multiple antennas to improve signal-to-noise ratio (diversity combining).

complex-square.title: Complex Square
complex-square.purpose: Squares the complex signal: z² = (Re + jIm)². This operation doubles all phase angles on the complex plane, which is a key property for processing modulated signals. For a BPSK signal (phases 0 and π), squaring 'collapses' both points into one (phases 0 and 2π = 0), enabling carrier frequency recovery. For QPSK, it removes two-fold ambiguity (4 points → 2 points).
complex-square.algorithm: Re_out = Re² - Im² Im_out = 2 · Re · Im Equivalent in polar coordinates: |z²| = |z|², arg(z²) = 2·arg(z).

examples.title: Costas Loop
examples.description: Signal → ComplexSquare → PLL → ComplexSqrt ComplexSquare removes BPSK modulation, PLL locks onto the doubled carrier, ComplexSqrt divides the frequency by two.

examples.title: Removing QPSK ambiguity
examples.description: QPSK → ComplexSquare → Constellation 4 QPSK points are transformed into 2 points (BPSK-like signal), simplifying further synchronization.

complex-sqrt.title: Complex Square Root
complex-sqrt.purpose: Computes the square root of a complex number via polar representation: √z = √|z| · exp(jθ/2). This operation halves phase angles — the inverse of ComplexSquare. Used in carrier recovery schemes where after squaring (frequency doubling), it is necessary to return to the original frequency by dividing by 2.
complex-sqrt.algorithm: r = sqrt(Re² + Im²)         — magnitude θ = atan2(Im, Re)           — argument (phase) Re_out = √r · cos(θ/2)     — real part of the root Im_out = √r · sin(θ/2)     — imaginary part of the root Returns the principal value of the root (branch with θ/2 ∈ [-π/2, π/2]).

examples.title: Carrier recovery (second stage)
examples.description: BPSK → ComplexSquare → PLL(2·fc) → ComplexSqrt PLL locks onto the doubled carrier, ComplexSqrt returns it to the original frequency fc.

examples.title: Nonlinear amplitude transformation
examples.description: Signal → ComplexSqrt → ComplexMagnitude → Oscilloscope Output amplitude = √|z| — dynamic range compression (analog of gamma correction with γ=0.5).

complex-phase.title: Phase (Complex)
complex-phase.purpose: Extracts the instantaneous phase of a complex signal: arg(z) = atan2(Im, Re). Converts a complex signal to real, preserving phase information and discarding amplitude. Instantaneous phase is a key concept in phase and frequency modulation/demodulation: the phase derivative over time gives instantaneous frequency, and phase jumps carry information in PSK modulation.
complex-phase.algorithm: y[n] = atan2(Im[n], Re[n]) Result in radians: from -π to +π. Phase 'wraps' at ±π transitions.

examples.title: Phase demodulation (PSK)
examples.description: PSK signal → PLL → ComplexPhase → Oscilloscope After synchronization, phase takes discrete values (e.g., 0, π/2, π, 3π/2 for QPSK).

examples.title: Computing instantaneous frequency
examples.description: Signal → ComplexPhase → derivative (diff) → scaling The phase difference of adjacent samples divided by 2π·dt gives the instantaneous signal frequency in Hz.

complex-magnitude.title: Magnitude (Complex)
complex-magnitude.purpose: Extracts the amplitude (magnitude) of a complex signal: |z| = sqrt(Re² + Im²). Converts a complex signal to real, preserving amplitude information and discarding phase. This is one of the most common operations when working with I/Q signals: envelope detection, AM demodulation, signal level measurement, spectrogram construction.
complex-magnitude.algorithm: y[n] = sqrt(Re[n]² + Im[n]²) Input array is interleaved: [Re0, Im0, Re1, Im1, ...], output is a regular real array.

examples.title: AM demodulation
examples.description: AM signal (I/Q) → ComplexMagnitude → Oscilloscope The complex envelope magnitude = original modulating signal.

examples.title: Level measurement after filtering
examples.description: Signal → BandpassFIR → ComplexMagnitude → NumericIndicator Shows the signal amplitude in the specified frequency band.

complex-composer.title: Complex Composer
complex-composer.purpose: Combines two real signals into one complex signal: the first input becomes the real part (Re), the second becomes the imaginary part (Im). This is the inverse operation of RealPart/ImagPart. This block is needed when I and Q components are generated separately (e.g., by separate Sine and Cosine generators) and need to be combined into a complex signal for further processing (filtering, constellation visualization, etc.).
complex-composer.algorithm: output[2n]     = Re[n]  (real part, upper input) output[2n + 1] = Im[n]  (imaginary part, lower input) If one input is not connected, the corresponding component = 0.
complex-composer.inputDescription: - Upper input (input 0): Re — real part - Lower input (input 1): Im — imaginary part Input: real (2 inputs, Float32Array)

examples.title: Manual I/Q formation
examples.description: Generator_I → [Re], Generator_Q → [Im] → ComplexComposer → Processing Allows creating a complex signal from arbitrary real components.

examples.title: Reassembling complex signal after separate processing
examples.description: Complex → RealPart → Filter → [Re] Complex → ImagPart → Filter → [Im] → ComplexComposer Separate I and Q filtering with subsequent recombination.

complex-conjugate.title: Complex Conjugate
complex-conjugate.purpose: Computes the complex conjugate signal by inverting the sign of the imaginary part of each sample. Geometrically, this is a reflection of the vector on the complex plane relative to the real axis. Conjugation is a fundamental DSP operation: it is used in correlation computation (x·conj(y)), matched filtering, autocorrelation function formation, and reversing the vector rotation direction.

examples.title: Spectrum reversal (mirroring)
examples.description: Signal → ComplexConjugate → SpectrumAnalyzer Conjugation reverses the frequency sign: if the signal rotated counterclockwise (+f), after conjugation it rotates clockwise (-f).

examples.title: Matched filter
examples.description: Known pattern → ComplexConjugate → ComplexMultiplier (×input) The basis of a correlation receiver for detecting a known signal in noise.

real-square.title: Square (Real)
real-square.purpose: Squares each sample of a real signal: y[n] = x[n]². Squaring is an important nonlinear DSP operation. For a sinusoid cos(2πft), the result contains a DC component and a harmonic at double frequency 2f (by the identity cos²(α) = (1 + cos(2α))/2). This property is used for frequency doubling and power detection.
real-square.algorithm: y[n] = x[n] · x[n] No parameters, no state.

examples.title: Power estimation
examples.description: Signal → RealSquare → LowpassFIR → NumericIndicator The mean value of x² is the root-mean-square power of the signal.

examples.title: Carrier recovery (BPSK)
examples.description: BPSK signal → RealSquare → BandpassFIR(2·fc) → Oscilloscope Squaring eliminates the ±1 modulation, leaving a component at 2·fc, from which the carrier is recovered by dividing the frequency by 2.

real-power4.title: Power of 4 (Real)
real-power4.purpose: Raises each sample of a real signal to the fourth power: y[n] = x[n]⁴. This nonlinear operation is widely used in spectral line methods for carrier frequency recovery from phase-modulated signals. If the input signal has M-PSK modulation with M=4 (QPSK), raising to the 4th power eliminates the phase modulation (all constellation points 'collapse' into one), and a spectral line appears at frequency 4·fc.
real-power4.algorithm: y[n] = x[n]² · x[n]² (two sequential multiplications for efficiency) No parameters, no state.

examples.title: Modulation analysis
examples.description: Unknown signal → RealPower4 → SpectrumAnalyzer If a peak at 4×f is visible, the signal is likely QPSK/4-QAM modulated. A peak at 2×f indicates BPSK, at 8×f — 8-PSK.

examples.title: Chain with frequency division
examples.description: QPSK → RealPower4 → BandpassFIR(4·fc) → frequency divider ÷4 Classic blind carrier recovery scheme in a demodulator.

atan2.title: Arctangent
atan2.purpose: Computes the angle (phase) in radians from two real inputs Y and X using the atan2(Y, X) function. Unlike the regular arctangent (atan), the atan2 function correctly determines the quadrant and returns a value in the full range [-π, π]. This is necessary for computing the instantaneous phase of a signal when the in-phase (I) and quadrature (Q) components are represented as separate real signals.
atan2.algorithm: y[n] = atan2(Y[n], X[n]) Result in radians: from -π (-180°) to +π (+180°). When Y=0 and X=0, the result is 0.
atan2.inputDescription: - Upper input (input 0): Y — vertical (imaginary) component - Lower input (input 1): X — horizontal (real) component Input: real (2 inputs, Float32Array)

examples.title: Direction detection
examples.description: Sine(f) → [Y], Cosine(f) → [X] → Atan2 → Oscilloscope The output is a linearly increasing phase (sawtooth signal) from -π to π, corresponding to vector rotation.

examples.title: Phase demodulation
examples.description: I-channel → [X], Q-channel → [Y] → Atan2 → differentiation Extracting instantaneous phase for subsequent instantaneous frequency computation (phase derivative over time).

agc.title: AGC
agc.purpose: Maintains a constant output signal level regardless of input level changes. AGC is widely used in radio receivers, audio systems, and telecommunications, where the input signal level can vary by tens of decibels. The block measures the instantaneous signal envelope and automatically adjusts the gain so that the RMS output level stays close to the target.
agc.algorithm: 1. Input signal envelope is computed using exponential smoothing: env += coeff · (|x[n]| - env). 2. Smoothing coefficient is chosen by attack/release principle: if |x| > env → attackCoeff is used (fast response to increase), otherwise → releaseCoeff (slow decay). 3. Gain: gain = min(targetLevel / env, maxGain). 4. Output: y[n] = x[n] · gain.

targetLevel.description: target output signal level. Range: 0.01–10. Usually 1.0 (normalized level).

attackTime.description: attack time. Determines how quickly the system responds to signal level increases. Smaller values → faster response to bursts but possible distortion. Range: 0.1–100 ms.
