releaseTime.description: release time. Determines how quickly gain increases when signal level decreases. Larger values ensure smoothness but slower adaptation. Range: 1–1000 ms.

maxGain.description: maximum allowed gain. Limits amplification of quiet segments (e.g., pauses/silence), preventing noise amplification. Range: 1–10000.

examples.title: Level stabilization in a receiver
examples.description: Antenna → Filter → AGC(target: 0.5, maxGain: 1000) → Demodulator Compensates for signal fading in the radio channel.

examples.title: Dynamic range compressor
examples.description: AudioFile → AGC(attack: 1ms, release: 100ms) → Speaker Fast attack limits peaks, slow release preserves natural sound.

absolute-value.title: Absolute Value
absolute-value.purpose: Computes the absolute value (magnitude) of each signal sample: y[n] = |x[n]|. In analog electronics, this is equivalent to a full-wave rectifier — negative half-waves are 'reflected' upward. The block is used for envelope detection (combined with an LPF), signal power measurement, and nonlinear transformations.
absolute-value.algorithm: y[n] = |x[n]| = Math.abs(x[n]) No parameters, no state — purely combinational operation.

examples.title: Spectral effects of rectification
examples.description: Sine(1000 Hz) → AbsoluteValue → SpectrumAnalyzer Instead of a single peak at 1 kHz, the spectrum shows a DC component and even harmonics (2 kHz, 4 kHz, ...) — the result of nonlinear transformation.

examples.title: Signal level measurement
examples.description: AudioFile → AbsoluteValue → Integrator → NumericIndicator Shows the mean absolute value (MAV) of the audio signal.

gain.title: Gain
gain.purpose: Multiplies each signal sample by a specified gain coefficient. This is the simplest yet one of the most frequently used DSP blocks. Gain is used for level matching between blocks, signal attenuation, phase inversion, and scale conversion. Unlike AGC, gain here is constant and set manually.
gain.algorithm: In linear mode: y[n] = x[n] · gain · (invert ? -1 : 1) In dB mode: linearGain = 10^(gaindB / 20), then y[n] = x[n] · linearGain dB formula: 0 dB = 1× gain (no change), +6 dB ≈ 2×, -6 dB ≈ 0.5×, +20 dB = 10×, -20 dB = 0.1×.

gain.description: gain coefficient. In linear mode: 0 = silence, 1.0 = no change, 2.0 = double. In dB mode: 0 = no change, -6 ≈ half, +20 = tenfold. Range: -100..+100 dB or 0..100 (linear).

gainMode.description: units: 'linear' — linear coefficient (dimensionless); 'dB' — decibels (logarithmic scale, convenient for large ranges).

invert.description: phase inversion (multiply by -1). Equivalent to a 180° phase shift. Used for forming an anti-phase signal in differential circuits.

examples.title: Phase inversion
examples.description: Sine → Gain(invert: true) → Summer (with original) The sum of a signal and its inverted copy gives zero — the principle of active noise cancellation.

examples.title: Level matching
examples.description: Weak signal → Gain(10.0, linear) → SpectrumAnalyzer 10× amplification before analysis for better visibility on the spectrogram.

log-exp.title: Logarithm/Exponential
log-exp.purpose: Applies one of five mathematical functions to each signal sample. Logarithmic functions are used for converting to decibel scale, dynamic range compression, and logarithmic scaling. Exponential functions are used for the inverse transformation (from dB to linear units) and modeling exponential processes (decay, growth).
log-exp.algorithm: - 'ln':    y = ln(max(|x|, ε))        — natural logarithm - 'log10': y = log₁₀(max(|x|, ε))     — common logarithm - 'dB':    y = 20·log₁₀(max(|x|, ε))  — decibels (voltage) - 'exp':   y = e^(min(x, 88))          — exponential (with overflow protection) - 'pow10': y = 10^(min(x, 38))         — power of 10 (with overflow protection) For logarithmic functions, |x| (absolute value) is taken and clamped from below by epsilon to avoid log(0) = -Infinity. For exponential functions, the argument is clamped from above to prevent Float32/Float64 overflow.

function.description: function selection: 'ln' — natural logarithm (base e ≈ 2.718); 'log10' — common logarithm (base 10); 'dB' — decibels: 20·log₁₀(|x|). For power, use 10·log₁₀; 'exp' — exponential e^x; 'pow10' — decimal exponential 10^x.

epsilon.description: minimum logarithm argument value. Prevents -Infinity when x=0 or very small values. Range: 1e-15–1e-3.

examples.title: Dynamic range compression
examples.description: AudioFile → LogExp(function: 'log10') → Oscilloscope Logarithmic display makes both loud and quiet signal segments visible.

examples.title: Inverse dB transformation
examples.description: Data in dB → LogExp(function: 'pow10') → Gain(0.05) Converts dB back to linear scale (with 1/20 correction).

mixer.title: Mixer
mixer.purpose: Multiplies the input real signal by a complex exponential exp(j·2π·f·t), performing spectrum translation (shift) to a specified frequency. This is a key operation in superheterodyne receivers, SDR (Software Defined Radio), and frequency multiplexing systems. The output is a complex (I/Q) signal representing the analytic image of the input signal shifted in frequency.
mixer.algorithm: I[n] = x[n] · cos(φ[n]) Q[n] = x[n] · sin(φ[n]) φ[n] = φ[n-1] + 2π · fShift / sampleRate Phase accumulates continuously from chunk to chunk and is normalized to [0, 2π) to prevent precision loss.

shiftFrequency.description: shift frequency. Positive values shift up in frequency, negative shift down. Range: -sampleRate/2 .. +sampleRate/2.

examples.title: Frequency conversion in a receiver
examples.description: Input signal → Mixer(-fc) → LowpassFIR → Demodulator Translating the radio signal from frequency fc to zero frequency (baseband) — standard SDR receiver operation.

examples.title: SSB (single-sideband) modulation
examples.description: AudioFile → Mixer(1500 Hz) → RealPart → SpectrumAnalyzer Translating the speech spectrum to the IF range. Taking the Re part gives a real signal with the upper sideband.

threshold.title: Comparator
threshold.purpose: Compares the input signal with a threshold level and produces a two-level (binary) output signal. In digital electronics, this is equivalent to a voltage comparator or Schmitt trigger (with hysteresis enabled). The comparator is used for converting an analog signal to a square wave, zero-crossing detection, clock pulse generation, and threshold processing.
threshold.algorithm: Without hysteresis: y[n] = x[n] > threshold ? outputHigh : outputLow With hysteresis (Schmitt trigger): - Upper threshold = threshold + hysteresis/2 - Lower threshold = threshold - hysteresis/2 - HIGH→LOW transition: only when x < lower threshold - LOW→HIGH transition: only when x > upper threshold Hysteresis prevents bouncing (rapid transitions) when a noisy signal slowly crosses the threshold.

threshold.description: threshold level. Center of the hysteresis zone. Range: any value.

outputHigh.description: output value when threshold is exceeded. Can be any number (not necessarily 0 or 1).

hysteresis.description: hysteresis zone width. 0 = simple comparator without hysteresis. Positive values create a 'dead zone' around the threshold. Recommended range: 0–1.

examples.title: Schmitt trigger for noisy signal
examples.description: Sine + Noise → Threshold(threshold: 0, hysteresis: 0.3) → Oscilloscope Hysteresis of 0.3 eliminates bouncing on switching edges.

examples.title: Level detector
examples.description: AudioFile → Threshold(threshold: 0.5, high: 1, low: -1) → NumericIndicator Determines moments when the signal exceeds the specified level.

oscilloscope.title: Oscilloscope
oscilloscope.purpose: The oscilloscope is the primary tool for visualizing signals in the time domain. It shows how the signal value (amplitude) changes over time. This block supports up to 4 independent channels, allowing simultaneous observation of multiple signals on one screen — for example, input and output signals of a filter, or I and Q components, or a signal before and after processing.
oscilloscope.algorithm: The block is 'transparent' (passthrough): it does not modify the input data but simply passes sample arrays from all connected channels to the OscilloscopeView visualization component. Data is packaged into an object {channels: [ch1, ch2, ch3, ch4]}, where each channel is a Float32Array or null (if input is not connected).
oscilloscope.outputDescription: null (visualization block, data is passed to OscilloscopeView)

timeWindow.description: display time window width in milliseconds. Determines how much data is visible on screen. Smaller value → more signal waveform detail. Larger value → overall envelope visible but fine details are lost.

examples.title: Comparing filter input and output
examples.description: Sine(1000) + NoiseGenerator → Summer → Oscilloscope (Channel 1) Summer → LowpassFIR(2000) → Oscilloscope (Channel 2) Channel 1 shows the noisy signal, Channel 2 shows it cleaned by the filter.

examples.title: Observing beats
examples.description: Sine(1000) → Oscilloscope (Channel 1) Sine(1050) → Oscilloscope (Channel 2) Sine(1000) → Summer ← Sine(1050), Summer → Oscilloscope (Channel 3) Channel 3 shows beats at 50 Hz (frequency difference).

constellation.title: Constellation Diagram
constellation.purpose: The constellation diagram is a way to visualize a digitally modulated signal. Each transmitted symbol is encoded by two numbers: I (in-phase component, horizontal) and Q (quadrature, vertical). On the diagram, each symbol is displayed as a point on the I/Q plane. For an ideal signal, points cluster at predetermined positions: - BPSK: 2 points on the horizontal axis (±1) - QPSK: 4 points at the corners of a square (±1 ± j1) - 8-PSK: 8 points on a circle - 16-QAM: 16 points in a 4×4 grid In real conditions, noise, distortions, and synchronization errors 'smear' the points around ideal positions. The degree of smearing indicates channel quality and demodulator correctness.
constellation.algorithm: The block is 'transparent' (passthrough) for the complex signal: it accepts interleaved Float32Array [I0, Q0, I1, Q1, ...] and passes it unchanged to the ConstellationView visualization component, which renders each (I, Q) pair as a point on a two-dimensional plane.
constellation.outputDescription: null (visualization block, data is passed to ConstellationView)

symbolRate.description: symbol rate in baud. Used by the visualizer to determine sampling instants (which samples are 'symbols').

constellation.description: constellation type. Options: 'BPSK', 'QPSK', '8PSK', '16QAM'. Determines the reference point grid displayed on the diagram.

eyeDiagram.description: eye diagram display. The eye diagram shows overlaid symbol intervals — the 'eye opening' indicates good signal quality.

examples.title: Evaluating noise impact
examples.description: PSKModulator(QPSK) → [noisy channel] → Constellation Points are 'smeared' around ideal positions. The stronger the noise, the larger the 'clouds' around each point.

examples.title: Synchronization verification
examples.description: PSKModulator(8PSK, sps=4) → TimingRecovery(sps=4) → PLL → Constellation If synchronization works correctly, 8 clear points on a circle are visible on the diagram. Without PLL, points rotate (phase offset).

waterfall.title: Waterfall
waterfall.purpose: The spectrogram (waterfall) is a two-dimensional display of the signal spectrum over time. Horizontally — frequency, vertically — time (new data 'flows' from top to bottom), the color of a point represents the amplitude at that frequency at that moment. This allows seeing how the signal's frequency content changes over time — something a regular spectrum analyzer cannot show (it displays only the current spectrum 'snapshot'). The spectrogram is invaluable for analyzing: - Speech and music (formants, harmonics, and rhythm are visible) - Frequency-modulated signals (frequency trajectory is visible) - Interference (short-term bursts are visible) - Frequency hopping signals
waterfall.algorithm: Processing is identical to SpectrumAnalyzer: 1. Input samples are written into a circular buffer of size fftSize. 2. Buffer contents are multiplied by a window function. 3. FFT is performed. 4. Magnitude is computed in decibels (computeMagnitudeDB). The difference is that each spectrum frame is passed to WaterfallView, which accumulates frames and renders a two-dimensional 'frequency × time' map.
waterfall.outputDescription: null (visualization block, data is passed to WaterfallView)

fftSize.description: FFT size. Determines frequency resolution: Δf = sampleRate / fftSize. Must be a power of two. Typical values: 512, 1024, 2048, 4096.

colorMap.description: color map for amplitude display. Determines which colors encode signal levels (e.g., dark colors = silence, bright colors = strong signal).

speed.description: waterfall scroll speed. Larger value → faster updates, more time resolution, but shorter visible history.

examples.title: Speech/music visualization
examples.description: AudioFile(speech.wav) → Waterfall(fftSize=4096) Characteristic horizontal bands — voice formants are visible, as well as pauses between words (dark areas).

examples.title: Detecting short-term interference
examples.description: Signal → Waterfall(speed=2) Short-term interference appears as a bright horizontal band at a specific frequency at a specific moment.

numeric-indicator.title: Numeric Indicator
numeric-indicator.purpose: Displays the instantaneous numeric value of a real signal. This is the simplest visualization block — analogous to a digital voltmeter: it shows the last signal sample as a number. Useful for monitoring constant values (DC), signal levels, computation results, and for debugging — to verify that the output value of a block matches expectations.
numeric-indicator.algorithm: The block is 'transparent' (passthrough): it accepts the input Float32Array unchanged and passes it to the NumericIndicatorView visualization component, which displays the last sample value in numeric format.
numeric-indicator.outputDescription: null (visualization block, data is passed to NumericIndicatorView)

examples.title: Signal level monitoring
examples.description: Sine(1000) → AmplitudeDetector → NumericIndicator Shows the current sine wave amplitude (≈1.0 at unity amplitude).

examples.title: Computation debugging
examples.description: Signal → Gain(coefficient=0.5) → NumericIndicator Verifies that the Gain block correctly scales the signal.

complex-numeric-indicator.title: Complex Numeric Indicator
complex-numeric-indicator.purpose: Displays the instantaneous value of a complex signal in Re + jIm format. A complex signal consists of two components: real (Re, I — in-phase) and imaginary (Im, Q — quadrature). This block shows both components simultaneously, which is convenient for debugging complex arithmetic, verifying modulator/demodulator operation, and monitoring phase relationships.
complex-numeric-indicator.algorithm: The block is 'transparent' (passthrough) for the complex signal: it accepts interleaved Float32Array [I0, Q0, I1, Q1, ...] unchanged and passes it to the visualization component, which displays the last (I, Q) pair in 'Re + jIm' format (e.g., '0.707 + j0.707').
complex-numeric-indicator.outputDescription: null (visualization block, data is passed to visualizer)

examples.title: Complex arithmetic verification
examples.description: ComplexComposer(Re=3, Im=4) → ComplexNumericIndicator The indicator shows '3.000 + j4.000' — convenient for verification.

examples.title: Demodulator debugging
examples.description: PSKModulator(QPSK) → PLL → ComplexNumericIndicator I and Q values should cluster around ±0.707 for QPSK — if not, synchronization is not working correctly.

multi-spectrum-analyzer.title: Multi-Channel Spectrum Analyzer
multi-spectrum-analyzer.purpose: Four independent spectrum analyzers on one screen. Allows simultaneous observation of spectra from multiple signals — for example, comparing spectrum before and after filtering, analyzing different processing branches, or monitoring multiple communication channels in parallel. Each channel performs a full spectral analysis cycle independently: its own circular buffer, window function, FFT, and averaging. Unconnected channels are not displayed.
multi-spectrum-analyzer.algorithm: Identical to the single-channel SpectrumAnalyzer: 1. Input samples are written into a circular buffer of size fftSize. 2. Buffer contents are multiplied by a window function. 3. Fast Fourier Transform (FFT) is performed. 4. Magnitude is computed (in dB or linear). 5. Exponential averaging is applied. Results from all channels are packaged into an object {channels: [ch1, ch2, ch3, ch4]}.
multi-spectrum-analyzer.outputDescription: null (visualization block, data is passed to MultiChannelSpectrumView)

fftSize.description: FFT size for all channels. Determines frequency resolution: Δf = sampleRate / fftSize. Must be a power of two. Typical values: 512, 1024, 2048, 4096.

averaging.description: number of exponential averaging frames. 1 = no averaging, 5–10 = smoothed spectrum.

examples.title: Monitoring multiple signals
examples.description: Sine(1000) → MultiChannelSpectrumAnalyzer (Channel 1) Sine(2000) → MultiChannelSpectrumAnalyzer (Channel 2) Sine(3000) → MultiChannelSpectrumAnalyzer (Channel 3) Sine(4000) → MultiChannelSpectrumAnalyzer (Channel 4) Each channel shows a peak at its frequency.

examples.title: Filter cascade analysis
examples.description: Signal → Filter1 → MultiChannelSpectrumAnalyzer (Channel 1) Filter1 → Filter2 → MultiChannelSpectrumAnalyzer (Channel 2) Allows evaluating each filter's contribution to the overall processing.

speaker.title: Speaker
speaker.purpose: Plays the input signal through the computer's audio system (speakers or headphones). This is the final block in a processing chain when the result needs to be not only seen but also heard. Used for listening to synthesized tones, demodulated signals, filtering effects, and any other audio processing results.
speaker.algorithm: The block itself is 'transparent' (passthrough): it returns the input sample array unchanged (or silence if mute is enabled). Actual audio playback is performed by DSPProcessor, which upon detecting a Speaker block in the graph directs its output data to the Web Audio API (AudioWorklet or ScriptProcessorNode). Sample rate is determined by simulation settings (default 48000 Hz). IMPORTANT: only one Speaker block can exist in the graph. When muted=true, the block outputs an array of zeros, resulting in silence at the output.
speaker.outputDescription: null (terminal block, data is directed to the audio system)

muted.description: mute audio. When true, the block outputs silence (Float32Array filled with zeros). Useful for temporarily disabling playback without breaking connections in the graph.

examples.title: Listening to filtering results
examples.description: AudioFile(music.wav) → NotchFIR(50 Hz) → Speaker Plays the audio file with 50 Hz mains hum suppressed.

examples.title: Demodulation and listening
examples.description: AMFMPMModulator(FM) → FrequencyDiscriminator → Speaker Recovers and plays the modulating signal from an FM signal. Warning: Signal amplitude must be within [-1, +1]. Values outside this range will cause clipping (distortion). If necessary, use the Gain block to scale the signal before feeding it to Speaker.
